status: DESIGN APPENDIX v3 (backlog): rows for milestones M3-M5 and 'post'. Not loaded by the game and not gated by the data test; a row moves into the live file, and under test, when its milestone starts. Rows may reference live ids.
id_rules: Ids are stable strings (prefix.name). Never rename an id once saves exist; add an alias instead. Display names are separate and may change. An id is defined in exactly one place: the live file or the backlog.

milestones.M1: A winter night: fire, shelter, cold, hunger, sleep, time safety; the fort region only; one background; 1765
milestones.M2a: A winter from the woods: living from the manor woods through the winter by your own hands (gathering, hides, sewing, snares, snowshoes, a half-faced camp, a hung cache, ice fishing); plain barter with the sutler, the trader, the garrison's soldiers, a farm family from German Flatts and an old hunter; credit and the fall outfit as options; the second background
milestones.M2b: Learning from neighbours: lessons, watching, examining, quality standards, haggling, promises and loans
milestones.M3: The year turns: the full almanac, seasons and weather content, the summer goal (bark and a cabin), fishing, frogs, ginseng, one played wage job; the fur cap and robe, leggings, carving, casting balls, the cache pit, char cloth and spruce beer
milestones.M4: People: NPC schedules and tiers at the fort, standing, invitations, the soldiers and the lieutenant as mentors; Native characters only after the relevant nation's sign-off
milestones.M5: The map: the Carry, the valley, the town and the hunting grounds, travel and camps, other markets and backgrounds
milestones.post: After M5 and not yet planned: the 1757 and 1761 starts and their eras, detailed illnesses, thirst, potash, upstream canoe and bateau travel, the Proxy NPC tier, languages beyond English, French, Mohawk and Oneida

source_keys.A: Bundled animation clip names and asset IDs
source_keys.N: graph_analysis/survival/survival_gdd.md, sources list (N:3 = source N3; N33 onward added in version 3)

basis_keys.S: sourced: checked against a primary source, a scholarly work or an institutional page; web summaries and popular pages do not qualify
basis_keys.H: standard historiography (books in the GDD sources list); verify before quoting
basis_keys.H-regional: true for one region's trade or society (named in the row); not yet checked for New York
basis_keys.M: modern science or medicine sets the mechanic (period explanation may differ)
basis_keys.D: design value for balance, or a figure resting on web summaries; not a checked historical record

livelihoods.name: Trading on credit (packhorse or post)
livelihoods.capital: goods on a merchant's consignment; one packhorse carries about 200 lb (E:S27)

unlock.licence: 1765-68: a licence and bond (Trade Master or a merchant's letter); after 1768 regulation is weak

livelihoods.history: Under the Plan of 1764 trade was meant to go through posts under commissaries and tariffs; after 1768 the colonies took regulation back and enforced it weakly (E:S7, N:21).
livelihoods.income_note: cash-equivalent pence; retune against the live ladder when the row goes live

livelihoods.name: Clearing land and homesteading
livelihoods.capital: a lease (entry fine and rent) or a lot bought from a patentee; axe, hoe, seed
livelihoods.notes: Corn feeds the household and sells dear in the hungry time; potash sold from the mid-1760s, when New York output grew, and far more after 1790. Harvest yields use the season-total scale (0.49).
risks: stock breaking into a town's corn
livelihoods.land_ethics: Squatting on a nation's unceded land or beyond the 1768 line costs standing and starts a dispute; Indian-deed fraud behind some patents is part of the world (event.deed_dispute).
livelihoods.history: Mohawk valley land came by patents, leases and purchases from patentees; Palatine German, Dutch and Scots-Irish families farmed it (N:13, N:21).
livelihoods.income_note: cash-equivalent pence; retune against the live ladder when the row goes live

livelihoods.name: Fishing the runs
livelihoods.history: Runs follow drainage: shad and herring only on the Hudson below Cohoes; fall salmon and eels on the Oneida Lake side of the Carry; eels and spring suckers everywhere (seasons.json fish_runs).
livelihoods.income_note: cash-equivalent pence; retune against the live ladder when the row goes live

livelihoods.name: Maple sugaring
livelihoods.notes: Also food for the lean weeks (1 lb of sugar is 340 game kcal) and a valued gift.
livelihoods.history: Developed by Native peoples of the Northeast; kettles made boiling easier; camps made sugar from late February to April (E:S54, E:S56).
livelihoods.income_note: cash-equivalent pence; retune against the live ladder when the row goes live

livelihoods.name: Gathering (ginseng, nuts, medicinal plants)
livelihoods.notes: Low income on its own; picked up while hunting or trapping.
livelihoods.history: Ginseng went from Montreal to Canton; Mohawk women helped identify it in 1716; the 1750s boom collapsed (E:S19).
livelihoods.income_note: cash-equivalent pence; retune against the live ladder when the row goes live

livelihoods.name: Supplying and serving the army
livelihoods.notes: In peace the detachment's firewood, fresh meat and small contracts through the sutler (live), with army wagon hire only in war starts (post). The discharged regular's spike: live in 1765.
livelihoods.history: The army hired civilian wagons and packhorses (Franklin, 1755); bateau men moved supplies; garrisons bought fresh food and game (E:S29, E:S58).
livelihoods.income_note: cash-equivalent pence; retune against the live ladder when the row goes live

livelihoods.name: Soldiering, ranging and scouting
livelihoods.notes: Steady pay, rations and a bounty in war years; scouts and expresses in peace. Obligations and danger.
livelihoods.history: Provincials enlisted for a campaign season (Anderson, A People's Army); rangers scouted on snowshoes and by whaleboat (K:2).
livelihoods.income_note: cash-equivalent pence; retune against the live ladder when the row goes live

livelihoods.name: Trades and services (carrying, boating, guiding, interpreting)
livelihoods.history: Oneida carriers and settler teamsters at the Carry (Roof's hauling from 1759), bateau crews on the Mohawk and Wood Creek, interpreters and smiths at posts (N:1, E:S7).
livelihoods.income_note: cash-equivalent pence; retune against the live ladder when the row goes live

livelihoods.name: Living a town household's seasonal round

unlock.standing: home town 40+ (the town-raised background starts there)

livelihoods.notes: Income comes in shares, food, lodging and standing rather than coin. The household decides what the player is invited to do; ceremonies stay with the community.
livelihoods.history: Towns stayed occupied through the year: the men's fall hunt, Midwinter at home, spring fishing and sugaring, women's fields, orchards and livestock (N:6, N:7, N:4).
livelihoods.income_note: cash-equivalent pence; retune against the live ladder when the row goes live

jobs.played: drive or escort the wagon along the military road; a time-skip rolls the losses instead

losses_per_trip.ambush: 0.04 x route danger x war mult

jobs.note: bateaux up the Mohawk, across the Carry on wagons or sledges, and down Wood Creek
In 1765 the post hires local woodsmen to scout or carry expresses; the half-pay lieutenant arranges it. Orders and ranging companies belong to the war starts (post).

jobs.time_skip_rule: needs tick through advance(); time_safety interrupts apply

jobs.note: a county bounty for wolves, an animal bounty only (E:S62); the game never offers bounties on people

jobs.pay: corn, sugar or moccasins; standing (npcs.json standing.sources.job)
a quarter of the day's sugar; may teach

v3_notes.trapping_history: v2 said most beaver in the 1750s-60s were taken by breaking into lodges, 'the usual 18th-century way', and that steel traps were scarce and dear. That rests on Carlos and Lewis (N:23), a study of the Hudson's Bay Company's lowland trade: tagged H-regional. Colonial smiths were making beaver traps for the 1760s Pennsylvania trade, and traps appear in traders' papers (N:36). The lodge hunt stays as one real method; check the Johnson Papers tariffs (1761, 1765), the Fort Pitt trading post papers (1757-65), the Baynton, Wharton and Morgan invoices and the Albany ledgers before fixing the trap stock cap.
